passage:
It was pouring, the school bus was twenty minutes late, and the maths exam started at nine. Aditi dug through her bag for the third time. The blue pen with the chewed cap, the one she had used for every test since Class 3, wasn't there.
"I'll fail," she said, and her voice wobbled.
Ishita held out a pen. "Take mine. It writes the same."
"It's not the same." Aditi's hands were cold. On the bus she kept counting: every test with the blue pen, good marks. Every time without... she couldn't remember a time without.
In the exam hall she wrote her name with Ishita's pen, very slowly. Then she read the first question and knew the answer.

qa.q: What was special about the pen Aditi couldn't find?
qa.a: It was the blue pen with the chewed cap, used for every test since Class 3.

qa.q: Why did Aditi's voice wobble when she said 'I'll fail'?
qa.a: Aditi felt scared because she truly believed the blue pen helped her score well, so losing it on a rushed, rainy morning felt like losing her luck. 😰

qa.q: What turning point in the exam hall could help Aditi trust herself instead of the pen?
qa.a: Knowing the first answer with Ishita's pen shows the maths was in her head, not in the pen; noticing that could loosen the routine's grip.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Aditi says 'It's not the same'?
qa.a: Ishita might feel a little brushed off, since the offer was kind, but also worried at seeing a friend's cold hands and wobbly voice.

grounding: A girl who loses her lucky pen on exam morning feels real panic, sure the pen decides her marks.

passage:
Before every under-12 match at the Kothrud ground, Lalit did the same things: left shoe first, three taps of the bat on the crease, and the corner seat on the team bench. He had scored fifty once after that routine, and since then he never skipped it.
On Saturday, Santosh got to the bench first and sat in the corner seat, swinging his legs.
"That's my seat," Lalit said.
"Seats aren't anyone's," said Santosh.
Lalit sat at the other end, knee bouncing. He tied his right shoe first by mistake and had to undo it. When he walked out to bat, his mouth was dry.
He was out for four. On the way back he glared at the corner seat.

qa.q: Where did Lalit usually sit on the team bench?
qa.a: Lalit sat in the corner seat on the team bench.

qa.q: Why was Lalit's mouth dry when he walked out to bat?
qa.a: Losing the corner seat and tying the wrong shoe first made him feel his luck was broken, and that worry walked out to the crease with him. 😰

qa.q: What could Lalit's coach help him try before the next match?
qa.a: The coach could help him build a routine about skills, like watching the bowler's hand and breathing slowly, which works from any seat.

qa.q: How might Santosh see Lalit's glare at the corner seat?
qa.a: Santosh just sat where there was space, so the glare might feel confusing and unfair to him.

grounding: A boy believes a fixed seat and shoe order decide his batting, and missing them makes him anxious before he is out.

passage:
"Aai, where's the curd?"
"Finished last night, Omkar. The milkman comes at eight."
"But my science exam is at eight-thirty! I always eat curd and sugar before exams!"
Tushar looked up from his phone. "Bhau, you got 62 in English. Did you eat curd that day?"
"...Yes."
"And 91 in maths?"
"Yes, but..."
"So the same curd gave you 62 and 91?"
Omkar's chin shook. "What if today goes wrong?"
Tushar put the phone down. "Then it'll be because of the magnets chapter, not the curd. Come, I'll quiz you."
Aai handed Omkar a spoon of plain sugar. "Half the ritual. The other half is already in your head. You studied."

qa.q: When does the milkman come?
qa.a: The milkman comes at eight.

qa.q: What does Omkar's shaking chin show about how he feels?
qa.a: It shows real fear: without the curd routine he believes the exam might go wrong, even after Tushar's questions.

qa.q: Which of Tushar's choices helped most in that moment?
qa.a: Putting the phone down and offering to quiz Omkar on magnets turned his attention from the missing curd to what he could actually control. 🙂

qa.q: How does Aai see the missing curd?
qa.a: Aai treats it gently, offering sugar as half the ritual while reminding Omkar that his studying matters more.

grounding: A boy panics when the curd for his pre-exam ritual runs out, sure it affects his marks, and his family steadies him.

passage:
I'm Zubin, and last year I believed chair number seven won my chess games. It was the wobbly one by the window at the Saturday chess club. I sat there, put my pencil to the left of the score sheet and tapped the table twice. I won four games in a row like that.
Then at the district junior tournament, a boy was already sitting in chair seven. My stomach went tight. I asked Afreen if we could swap tables. She said, "The chair doesn't know chess." I lost my first game in twenty moves because I kept thinking about the chair.
In the second game I made myself look only at the board, not the window. I won. I still tap the table sometimes, but now I know my openings did the work.

qa.q: Which chair did Zubin believe won the chess games?
qa.a: Chair number seven, the wobbly one by the window at the Saturday chess club.

qa.q: How can you tell that losing the special seat made Zubin anxious?
qa.a: Zubin's stomach went tight, Zubin asked to swap tables, and Zubin kept thinking about the chair while losing the first game in twenty moves.

qa.q: What turning point helped Zubin in the second game?
qa.a: Choosing to look only at the board; putting attention on the moves showed that the openings, not the chair, were doing the work.

qa.q: How does Afreen see the chair routine, and why might Afreen say it so bluntly?
qa.a: Afreen sees the chair as having nothing to do with winning, and probably wants Zubin to stop worrying about the seat and get back to thinking about the game.

grounding: It shows a child who believes a special seat and routine decide chess results and feels real anxiety when the seat is taken.

passage:
Coach's notes, Saturday swim meet (Neelam)
Swati, 10, arrived pale today. She had left her faded red cap at home, the one she has worn at every race since spring. She told me she can't swim fast without it, and that she always touches the wall three times and says her lane number before diving. Her hands were shaking. She asked to drop out of the 50 metres.
I didn't argue about the cap. I asked what she does in the last ten metres. "Kick harder, no breathing," she said. We practised her start twice in the warm-up lane in a borrowed cap.
She swam, a second slower than her best, and said, "Maybe the cap is only for luck."
Next: talk with her parents about a pre-race routine she controls: breathing, stretches, the start.

qa.q: What had Swati left at home?
qa.a: Her faded red cap, the one she has worn at every race since spring.

qa.q: Why did forgetting the cap feel so frightening to Swati?
qa.a: Swati believed the cap and the wall-touching helped her swim fast, so without them the race felt out of her control; her pale face and shaking hands show how real the worry was 😰

qa.q: Which choice by Coach Neelam helped Swati decide to swim?
qa.a: Instead of arguing about the cap, Neelam asked about Swati's own last ten metres and practised her start, turning attention to things Swati actually controls.

qa.q: What would change if the coach had simply said, "Caps don't matter, get in the water"?
qa.a: Swati might have felt brushed aside and more anxious, and could have dropped out, because her worry would be dismissed rather than steered toward what she can do.

grounding: It shows a child relying on a lucky cap and wall-touching routine before races and feeling real anxiety when the cap is missing.

passage: Before every test I use my green pen, the one I got for my birthday. I got full marks in the first spelling test with it, so I knew it was lucky. Last week, on the morning of the maths exam, I couldn't find it. I looked under my bed, in my bag, even in the fridge. I started crying at the school gate, and my stomach felt full of bees. Aditi, who sits next to me, gave me her blue pen. "It writes the same," she said. I was sure I would fail. Then I started the sums and forgot about the pen. I got 18 out of 20. Mummy found the green pen in my raincoat pocket that evening. Now I think the pen isn't lucky. Rajni just knows her tables.

qa.q: What mark did Rajni get in the maths exam?
qa.a: 18 out of 20.

qa.q: How did Rajni feel at the gate without the green pen?
qa.a: She felt anxious and scared, crying, with her stomach full of bees, sure she would fail without the lucky pen.

qa.q: What could help Rajni before the next test?
qa.a: Remembering that she scored 18 with Aditi's blue pen, so her practice, not the pen, earns the marks.

qa.q: What was it like for Aditi to lend her pen?
qa.a: Aditi was kind and calm, simply offering a pen that writes the same.

grounding: A girl recalls believing her green pen made her do well and panicking when it went missing before an exam.

passage:
Swimming coach's note, district trials, Saturday
Hansa (10-12 age group) has a routine before every race: she touches the starting block three times, fixes her cap twice, and always swims in lane four. Today the officials put her in lane two. She went pale, said, "I'll lose now," and her hands shook on the block. Devika, from our club, told her lane two was "just water, same as four." I sat with Hansa for two minutes and asked her to count her breaths, not her touches. She swam and finished second, one second faster than her best. Afterwards she asked me, "So lane four isn't magic?" I told her it was her training that made her fast. We will practise in different lanes this week.

qa.q: Which lane does Hansa always swim in?
qa.a: Lane four.

qa.q: Why did Hansa go pale when put in lane two?
qa.a: She felt anxious and frightened that missing her usual lane meant she would lose.

qa.q: What did the coach do, and what is the plan for the week?
qa.a: Helped her count breaths instead of touches, then planned practice in different lanes so the routine loses its hold.

qa.q: How did Devika try to help?
qa.a: Devika calmly told Hansa that lane two was just water, same as four.

grounding: A swimming coach records a girl who believes her lane and routine decide her races, and panics when they change.

passage:
Saturday
Big match day. I always sit in the third seat on the left on the school bus before a match, because that's where I sat when we won the zonal final. Today Lokesh bhaiya drove me in the car instead because the bus was late. No third seat. I felt sick the whole way. I kept thinking, that's it, we'll lose, and it'll be my fault.
We won. By forty runs. I took two catches.
Now I'm lying here thinking. The seat wasn't there, and we still won. So maybe it was never the seat. Maybe it was the nets practice every evening.
I'm still going to sit there next time. But maybe I won't cry if I can't.
Usha

qa.q: How many catches did Usha take?
qa.a: Two catches.

qa.q: How did Usha feel in the car?
qa.a: Usha felt sick and anxious the whole way, sure the team would lose and it would be Usha's fault.

qa.q: What does Usha start to realise, and how could it help next time?
qa.a: That the win came from nets practice, not the seat, which could ease the panic if the seat isn't there again.

qa.q: Why might Lokesh bhaiya have been puzzled by Usha's mood?
qa.a: Lokesh bhaiya was only giving a lift because the bus was late, not knowing how much the seat mattered to Usha.

grounding: A child's diary shows panic at missing a lucky bus seat before a match, and the win that followed anyway.

passage: On the morning of the Class 6 half-yearly exam in the government school at Jalna, Tanuja opened her pencil box and froze. The blue pen was gone. Her lucky pen. She had written every good test with it since Class 4. Without it, her hands went cold. "I'll fail," she whispered to Alka on the bench. "It's just a pen," Alka said, holding out a spare one. Tanuja shook her head. The bell rang. The papers came. For the first ten minutes she couldn't read the questions properly; her heart was too loud. Then she forced herself to start with Alka's pen. She knew the answers. They were in her head, not in the pen. She walked out tired, and feeling almost silly.

qa.q: What had Tanuja written every good test with since Class 4?
qa.a: The blue pen, her lucky pen.

qa.q: What was Tanuja feeling when she found the pen was gone?
qa.a: She felt panicked, hands cold and heart loud, sure she would fail without her lucky pen.

qa.q: What could Tanuja remind herself before the next exam?
qa.a: That the answers are in her head, not in the pen, so any pen will do and she can focus on what she studied.

qa.q: How does Alka see the lost pen?
qa.a: Alka sees it as just a pen and calmly offers a spare, not sharing Tanuja's worry.

grounding: Shows a child believing her lucky pen affects her exam results and feeling real anxiety when it goes missing.

passage: Amara always wore the same yellow socks for football matches in Nairobi. Unwashed, never changed, stuffed in the corner of her bag. Her team had won four games in a row with those socks. On Saturday morning, she opened her bag at the pitch. No socks. Her mother had washed them. Amara's stomach dropped. "We're going to lose," she told Marek, the goalkeeper. "It's my fault." Marek shrugged. "I wear the same gloves every time and we lost twice last month." Amara didn't hear him. She played the first half badly, looking at her white socks, missing passes. At half-time, the coach sat beside her. "What wins matches?" Amara mumbled, "Passing. Running." "Can socks do that?" Amara thought about it. In the second half she played properly. They drew, one-all.

qa.q: What colour were Amara's match socks?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: Why did Amara play the first half badly?
qa.a: She felt anxious and guilty, convinced the missing socks would make the team lose and distracted by worrying about them.

qa.q: How did the coach help Amara at half-time?
qa.a: The coach asked what really wins matches, passing and running, which turned her attention back to what she controls.

qa.q: How does Marek see lucky kit?
qa.a: Marek doesn't trust it much, since he wears the same gloves and they still lost twice last month.

grounding: Shows a child who believes her unwashed match socks affect results and feels real anxiety when they go missing.

passage: At the chess club in the Pune community centre, Chaitanya always sat at table seven, by the window. He had won every tournament game from that seat. On Sunday he arrived and a new boy was already sitting there. Chaitanya stood frozen. The organiser, Bhavna didi, pointed to table three. "Sit there, games start in two minutes." "I can't," Chaitanya whispered. "Table seven is my table." His chest was tight. He sat at table three, but he kept glancing at the window. He lost in twenty moves. "Wrong table," he told Bhavna didi afterwards, eyes wet. She took out his scoresheet. "Look at move eight. You didn't see my bishop. That's not the table." Chaitanya read it twice. Next week he asked to sit at a different table on purpose.

qa.q: Which table did Chaitanya always sit at?
qa.a: Table seven, by the window.

qa.q: What was Chaitanya feeling when he saw the new boy at table seven?
qa.a: He felt panicked and tight in the chest, sure he couldn't win without his usual seat.

qa.q: How did Bhavna didi help, and what did Chaitanya try next?
qa.a: She showed him the real mistake on his scoresheet; next week he chose a different table on purpose to test the belief.

qa.q: How might the new boy at table seven feel if he knew?
qa.a: The new boy would probably be surprised, having no idea the seat meant so much to Chaitanya.

grounding: Shows a child who believes his special seat affects his chess results and feels real anxiety when he cannot use it.

passage:
Monday, the first cold morning of the December exams. Nitin tapped his blue pen three times on the desk before writing his name, like always. Maths went well. Of course it did.
Wednesday. The blue pen was gone. Nitin tipped his bag out on the bench, stomach tight. "I can't write Science without it," he told Darshan. His hands were shaking.
Darshan held out a green pen. "It's just ink."
Nitin wrote the whole paper with it, sure every answer was going wrong.
The next Monday, the papers came back. Maths: 41. Science, the green-pen paper: 43.
Nitin looked at the two numbers for a long time. Then he found the blue pen in his winter jacket pocket and dropped it in his pencil box like any other pen.

qa.q: What was Nitin feeling on Wednesday when the pen was missing?

qa.q: What could help Nitin before the next exam?

passage:
Abhinav, you think your lucky socks win matches? Let me tell you about my lucky stone.
When I was your age, our village played football against the next village every Bohag Bihu. One year I found a smooth white stone by the river and kept it in my pocket. We won. Next Bihu I carried it again. We won again. By then I was sure the stone was our best striker.
The third year, on match morning, it was gone. I cried behind the granary. My legs shook so much I missed an easy pass.
At half-time our captain grabbed my shoulders. "Bhupen, you trained all month. Your legs know. The stone doesn't."
I played the second half thinking only about the ball. We drew, but I scored.
The stone turned up a week later, in my mother's washing basket.

qa.q: Where did Bhupen find the white stone?
qa.a: Bhupen found the smooth white stone by the river.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling on the morning the stone went missing?
qa.a: Bhupen felt panicky and afraid, crying behind the granary and shaking so much that an easy pass was missed.

qa.q: Which moment in the story turned the match around for Bhupen, and why?
qa.a: The captain's reminder that Bhupen's legs knew the training, not the stone, shifted the focus to the ball, and Bhupen scored.

qa.q: How might the captain have seen Bhupen at half-time?
qa.a: The captain probably saw a teammate frozen by worry and knew a firm, kind reminder of the training could steady Bhupen.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling a childhood lucky stone that seemed to decide matches and the real anxiety of losing it.

passage:
The monsoon had flooded the main road, so the school van didn't come on the morning of the inter-school spelling bee.
"Auto," said Rekha, grabbing her umbrella and Suraj's hand.
Suraj's chest went tight. Every time he had won a spelling round, he had sat in the third seat of the van, left side, and counted the lamp posts to school. Twenty-two. No van, no third seat, no counting.
"I'll lose," he whispered as the auto splashed through a puddle. "I always count."
"Count now," Rekha said.
"It's different. The auto goes a different way."
Rekha thought for a second. "Then spell the words on the shop signs instead. That's practice, not magic."
Suraj spelled pharmacy, jewellers, stationery. His voice was still wobbly when they reached the hall.

qa.q: How many lamp posts did Suraj usually count on the way to school?
qa.a: Suraj counted twenty-two lamp posts.

qa.q: Why did Suraj's chest go tight when the van didn't come?
qa.a: Suraj felt anxious, because the third seat and the counting felt like what made him win, and without them he was sure he'd lose.

qa.q: Which idea of Rekha's helped, and why?
qa.a: Spelling the words on shop signs gave Suraj real practice instead of a ritual, turning the worry into something useful.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Rekha?
qa.a: Rekha had to manage a flooded road and an auto, and still quickly found a way to steady Suraj without laughing at the routine.

grounding: Shows a child whose fixed seat and counting routine before a spelling bee is broken by the monsoon, bringing real anxiety.

passage: On the morning of his December maths exam, Yash couldn't find his lucky blue pen, the one with the chewed cap he had used in every test since class three. He tipped his whole school bag onto the bed. Not there. His chest tightened. "I'll fail without it," he said, near tears. His sister Ganga held out two new pens. "They write the same." "No! The blue one knows the answers." Their mother found it in the pocket of his winter jacket, and Yash clutched it all the way to school in the foggy auto. The exam went well. "Told you," he said that evening. Ganga didn't mention that he had also studied every single evening for two weeks.

qa.q: Where did their mother find the lucky blue pen?
qa.a: In the pocket of his winter jacket.

qa.q: Why did Yash feel he would fail without the blue pen?
qa.a: He believed the pen affected his results, so losing it made him anxious and near tears, as if part of his control had gone.

qa.q: What could help Yash feel steady even without the pen?
qa.a: He could notice what really helped, like studying every evening for two weeks, and practise a test at home with a different pen first.

qa.q: How does Ganga see the lucky pen?
qa.a: Ganga sees it as an ordinary pen and knows the two weeks of study mattered, though she chooses not to argue.

grounding: Shows a child who believes a lucky pen affects his exam results and feels real anxiety when it goes missing.
